questions.q: What are the four phases of the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle, in order?
options: Detection, Preparation, Recovery, Containment
Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
Planning, Coding, Testing, Deployment
Triage, Prioritize, Remediate, Verify
questions.explain: NIST SP 800-61 defines the lifecycle as Preparation, Detection and Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, and Post-Incident Activity.

questions.q: What belongs in the Preparation phase?
options: Rotating the credentials that were compromised
Writing the postmortem after the incident is resolved
Monitoring and logging, a defined response team, and a rehearsed communication plan, all done before an incident occurs
Determining whether an alert represents a real incident
questions.explain: Preparation covers everything done before an incident happens: tooling, team readiness, and a plan that's been rehearsed, not improvised in the moment.

questions.q: Why are Containment, Eradication, and Recovery grouped into a single phase rather than three separate ones?
options: Because only containment actually matters
Because they often happen in overlapping, iterative steps rather than a strict one-after-another sequence
Because NIST SP 800-61 does not define eradication or recovery
Because they are performed by entirely different teams with no coordination
questions.explain: The lesson groups these because in practice a response team cycles through stopping the spread, removing the cause, and restoring service in overlapping steps, not a rigid sequence.

questions.q: Why is the incident response lifecycle described as 'a loop, not a line'?
options: Because incidents repeat identically every time
Because Post-Incident Activity's findings feed back into Preparation, making the next incident cheaper to handle
Because Detection and Analysis happens twice in every incident
Because NIST requires exactly two incidents per year
questions.explain: The entire value of the Post-Incident Activity phase is that its lessons become new monitoring rules, runbook updates, or training — feeding directly back into Preparation.

questions.q: In the Northbridge Retail example, what was identified as the root cause during Eradication?
options: A misconfigured firewall rule
A leaked API key that let an identity read data it normally only wrote
An expired TLS certificate
A missing disk encryption setting
questions.explain: The team traced the anomalous read activity to a leaked API key, which they rotated during Eradication before restoring service with a freshly scoped identity.
